query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Removing or reducing the superficial microstructural heterogeneities (such as inclusions and oxide discontinuities) via mechanical surface polishing will delay or suppress the localized initiation of corrosion on pre‐exposure Q235 steel in harsh, chloride‐containing environments at both room and elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 carbon steel in its as-received (pre-exposure) condition, containing its natural heterogeneous microstructure with inclusions, grain-boundary irregularities, and a native oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Mechanical surface polishing of the Q235 steel to remove surface irregularities and inclusions while maintaining the bulk properties.
generation.conditions: Expose both polished and unpolished Q235 steel samples to a controlled harsh corrosive environment (e.g., a 3.5 wt.% NaCl aqueous solution) at room temperature and at an elevated temperature (with the exact temperature controlled via a laboratory oven), while maintaining other variables (pH, flow, and exposure time) constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The density and continuity of the surface oxide film and the presence of microstructural defects (inclusions and grain-boundary sites) that act as localized anodic regions for corrosion initiation.
generation.mechanism: Surface heterogeneities on untreated Q235 steel serve as preferential sites for localized anodic reactions (galvanic cells) when exposed to chloride ions. Polishing reduces these heterogeneities, leading to a more uniform, possibly more protective, oxide layer that retards the initiation and progression of pitting or other localized corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated (unpolished) reference, mechanically polished Q235 steel will exhibit a lower corrosion rate (e.g., reduced weight loss), lower pitting density, and a higher (more noble) corrosion potential in electrochemical tests under the same harsh environmental conditions.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel in the original, pre-exposure state without any surface modification, exposed to the same chloride solution at the same temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under corrosive conditions typical of a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at controlled room and elevated temperatures; effects outside these controlled conditions (such as in environments with different chemical compositions or extreme temperatures) are not addressed.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement (e.g., percentage reduction in corrosion rate) due to polishing is uncertain, as it depends on the initial defect density and the effectiveness of the polishing process. Additionally, the stability of the newly formed oxide film at elevated temperatures may vary and warrants further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel coupons from the same batch: one set with a standard mechanical polishing treatment to remove surface defects, and an unpolished control set. Immerse both sets in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under identical conditions at room temperature and at a predetermined elevated temperature. Monitor the corrosion behavior over time by performing weight loss measurements, electrochemical tests (such as Tafel polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy), and microscopic examination (to assess pitting density and morphology).
measurements: Weight change (loss or gain) over fixed time intervals
Corrosion potential and current density from potentiodynamic polarization tests
Electrochemical impedance (Rct values) from EIS studies
Pitting density and morphology via optical or scanning electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the polished Q235 steel samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (i.e., lower corrosion rate, higher corrosion potential, and reduced pitting density) compared to the unpolished controls under both room and elevated temperature conditions, then the hypothesis that surface heterogeneity reduction suppresses corrosion initiation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: (1) The (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating was prepared by plasma spraying on substrate of the Q235 steel, consisting of a simple FCC solid solution with Laves phase, and the coating bonded well to the substrate. (2) Elemental segregation occurred between the dendrites and the interdendrites of the coating, and the elements Cr and Nb with high melting point were enriched between the interdendrites. This phenomenon may be due to the difference in melting point of the element and the characteristics of the plasma spraying process. (3) The coating has a microhardness of 321 HV0.5, which can effectively improve the surface hardness of the Q235 steel part. (4) The (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating exhibited excellent corrosion resistance in the electrochemical corrosion test of a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution comparing to previously studied coatings prepared by other processes. (5) In the 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution, the selective corrosion occurred on the surface of (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating, while the interdendritic phase rich in Nb and Cr was preferentially corroded as an anode, and the dendritic phase rich in Co, Ni, and Fe was protected as a cathode.

In this paper, the CoCrFeNiTix HEA coatings are prepared on Q235 steel substrate by laser cladding. The effect of Ti content on the microstructure and corrosion resistance in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution was studied. Furthermore, the corrosion resistance mechanism was analyzed experimentally and by first-principles calculations.
